questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Konjunktiv I in reported speech
questions.learningObjective: choose the first-subjunctive form of a verb whose present differs from it
questions.stem: A pupil writes down what a colleague said as 'Er sagt, sie sei krank.' Why is that the right way to report the remark?

options.text: A report takes the first subjunctive, and sein forms that as sei against the present er ist
A report takes the second subjunctive, so sei would belong to an imagined case
options.misconception: believes German reported speech uses the second subjunctive

options.text: Sei is the plural form of sein, so the reported subject must have been a group
options.misconception: reads sei as a person and number form rather than a mood

options.text: Sei is the passive of sein, so the report makes its subject inactive
options.misconception: believes the reported clause has been turned into the passive

questions.explanation: German reports what another person said with the first subjunctive, and the verbs whose present form differs from the indicative are the ones that make the mood visible: sein gives sei against er ist, haben gives habe against er hat, and the modals and the verbs of knowing follow the same pattern, so können becomes könne. Where the first subjunctive happens to be spelled like the present, as with kommen in er sagt, er komme against er kommt, the mood simply is not marked in the letters and the reader takes it from the reporting verb. The trap is the second subjunctive, which is built from würde plus an infinitive and is reserved for what is imagined rather than reported, so a learner who reaches for it turns a quotation into a guess.
questions.hint: Ask whether the clause is quoting somebody or describing a situation that did not happen.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Konjunktiv I in reported speech
questions.learningObjective: recognise that a reported strong verb keeps the first-subjunctive shape
questions.stem: A report reads 'Der Kollege behauptet, er nehme den Zug nach Basel.' Which pair of forms justifies the shape nehme?

options.text: Nehmen gives nehme in the first subjunctive, and the present of the same verb is er nimmt
Nehmen gives nähme in the first subjunctive, and the present of the same verb is er nehme
options.misconception: believes the umlaut of nähme belongs to a report rather than to an imagined case

options.text: Nehmen gives nehme in the second subjunctive, and the present of the same verb is er nimmt
options.misconception: confuses the two subjunctives and applies the second to a reported claim

options.text: Nehmen gives nömme in the first subjunctive, and the present of the same verb is er nimmst
options.misconception: believes a reported third person singular keeps the ending of the du present

questions.explanation: A strong verb forms the first subjunctive by taking the vowel of the second person plural, so from ihr nehmt the third person singular comes nehme, while the present of the same verb is er nimmt and du nimmst. The umlaut a learner expects to see in a subjunctive belongs to the second subjunctive instead, so nähme and nömme are imagined forms and would turn a firm report into a guess about what somebody might do. The first subjunctive also lets a speaker pass a claim on without endorsing it, which is why such a report is usually introduced by behauptet, erklärt or sagt and not by wissen, since a speaker who knew the matter would say it as a fact.
questions.hint: Ask which form of the present the first subjunctive takes its vowel from.

questions.topic: Konjunktiv I in reported speech
questions.learningObjective: read two versions of a report and say what the loss of the mood costs
questions.stem: A notice reads 'Der Sprecher sagt, der Zug habe Verspätung.' and a colleague retells it as 'Der Sprecher sagt, der Zug hat Verspätung.' What has the second version done?

options.text: It has dropped the reported mood, so the colleague now puts his own name to the delay
It has kept the reported mood, because haben and hat are one and the same form
options.misconception: believes the first subjunctive of haben is spelled exactly like the present

options.text: It has turned the report into a wish, so the delay is now presented as wanted
options.misconception: believes a clause that loses its subjunctive ending becomes a wish

options.text: It has moved the delay into the past, so the notice now reports it as finished
options.misconception: believes dropping a subjunctive ending signals a change of time

questions.explanation: Haben forms the first subjunctive as habe, which is visibly different from the present hat, so the first version keeps the reader one remove from the claim. When the colleague writes hat instead, the reporting frame stays but the mood is gone, and the sentence now reads as the colleague's own assertion, which in a notice means that somebody has taken responsibility for the delay. Nothing about the time has changed, since both versions are present, and what has changed is commitment rather than tense. That is also why reports that must stay neutral tend to prefer a past form such as wurde, because a past keeps the delay at a distance even when the reporting verb is dropped.
questions.hint: Ask who is standing behind the claim once the mood has gone.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Konjunktiv I form building
questions.learningObjective: explain how a first-subjunctive form is built and where it stops being visible
questions.stem: A learner asks how a first-subjunctive form is built and why two reported sentences look exactly like the present. Explain the two steps, and say what happens in a report when the two shapes collide.

answer.exemplar: Take the second person plural of the present, drop its ending and add the thematic vowel, then use the ending of the person you need: from ihr habt comes the singular habe, used for ich and er alike, while sein gives sei for both singular persons and seien for the plural. The strong verbs follow suit because the vowel of the plural survives, so ihr nehmt gives er nehme. Where the two shapes collide, as with kommen, sehen and sagen, the mood cannot be seen in the letters, and the expected result is a switch to the second subjunctive, as in 'Der Trainer sagt, das Spiel wäre hart' or 'Der Trainer sagt, das Spiel würde hart sein'.

questions.explanation: The rule has two steps, and the first is the one learners miss. A strong verb takes its first-subjunctive vowel from the second person plural, so ihr nehmt supplies the e in er nehme, and the endings of the three singular persons are then -e, -est and -e, which is why the first and third person singular look alike. The second step is that sein, haben and the modals and the verbs of knowing drop the infinitive ending and take the thematic vowel, so sein gives sei and seien, haben gives habe, and können gives könne. Where the resulting form is identical to the present, as with kommen and sagen, the first subjunctive is no longer visible in writing, and that is precisely the case a course has to talk about. The remedy is the second subjunctive, in the bare form with the umlaut or in the würde form, because both can be seen on the page.
questions.hint: Ask which form of the present the first subjunctive takes its vowel from.

questions.learningObjective: mark a condition the speaker knows is not the case
questions.stem: A speaker says 'Wenn ich mehr Zeit hätte, würde ich einen Sprachkurs besuchen.' What is the speaker doing with hätte?

options.text: Presenting a condition the speaker knows to be untrue, so the sentence ends in a wish
Presenting a condition the speaker is certain about, so the sentence reports a known fact
options.misconception: believes the second subjunctive can report a condition treated as certain

options.text: Presenting a question the speaker wants answered about the days ahead of them
options.misconception: believes a second-subjunctive clause marks a question about coming events

options.text: Presenting an order the speaker expects the listener to carry out at once
options.misconception: believes a subjunctive form can carry an instruction in the imperative sense

questions.explanation: The second subjunctive marks what is imagined rather than given, and a condition built with it tells the reader that the speaker does not hold the condition to be true. Hätte is built from hätt, the second-subjunctive stem of haben, and stands in for a present the speaker knows is not there. A real condition takes the ordinary present instead, as in Wenn ich heute Zeit habe, gehe ich schwimmen, and the difference between the two sentences is not about the future but about how firmly the speaker asserts the condition. The trap is a learner who reads the mood as doubt; the mood marks the condition as counterfactual, and any real uncertainty about it would be expressed by a modal such as vielleicht or by a conditional.
questions.hint: Ask whether the speaker believes the condition has come true.

questions.learningObjective: soften a request with the second subjunctive of a modal
questions.stem: A colleague needs a file and writes 'Könntest du mir den Bericht bis Freitag schicken?' Which word does the softening work?

options.text: Könntest, which is the second-subjunctive form of können and turns a demand into a request
Du, which is the informal address form and therefore softer than Sie in this context
options.misconception: believes the choice between du and Sie carries the politeness of this sentence

options.text: Bis Freitag, which gives the request a firm deadline and so lowers the pressure on the reader
options.misconception: believes a stated deadline makes a request more polite rather than more pressing

options.text: Mir, which is a dative form and marks the request as directed at a third person
options.misconception: believes the dative pronoun itself supplies the softening of a request

questions.explanation: Könntest is the second subjunctive of the modal können, with the ending -est added to the stem könn-, and a subjunctive on a modal turns an assertion of ability into a request. The plain form Kannst du mir den Bericht schicken asks whether the reader is able, while the subjunctive asks the reader to do it, which is why the mood does the work of softening rather than the choice of address form. A learner who swapped in Sie would still be polite but would be addressing a stranger or a superior, and a learner who left the mood out gets a demand. The same move works with the other modals, so Würdest du, Hättest du and Möchtest du all open a sentence that the present states flatly.
questions.hint: Ask whether the sentence reports an ability or asks for an action.

questions.learningObjective: compare two second-subjunctive variants and judge which is acceptable
questions.stem: A draft of a report reads 'Wenn wir mehr Zeit hätten, würden wir die Arbeit früher abgeben.' A colleague proposes 'Wenn wir mehr Zeit hätten, wir würden die Arbeit früher abgeben.' What is the verdict on the pair?

options.text: Only the first is acceptable, because a subordinate clause with two finite verbs ends with one
Both are acceptable, because a modal may stand in any position inside a subordinate clause
options.misconception: believes a subordinate clause allows its finite verb in any position

options.text: Neither is acceptable, because a second-subjunctive form may not follow a conjunction
options.misconception: believes a second-subjunctive form cannot appear after a conjunction at all

options.text: Only the second is acceptable, because the modal belongs directly after the conjunction
options.misconception: believes a subordinate clause requires the modal in the first position

questions.explanation: A subordinate clause with two finite verbs places the conjugated one at the end, so the modal in the second position goes to the close of the clause and only the infinitive follows it. That is why the first version works and the second does not: in the second the modal would be a finite verb in a position the clause does not offer. The rule is the mirror image of the main clause, where the conjugated verb takes the second position and everything else follows it. A learner who borrows the freedom of the main clause produces exactly this error, because the two positions feel interchangeable when the sentence is spoken and only the last one is available in writing.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Konjunktiv II in a wish
questions.learningObjective: state a wish that the speaker treats as unreal
questions.stem: A speaker says 'Wenn ich nur mehr Zeit hätte!' What kind of sentence is that?

options.text: An elliptical wish, because the clause stops at the second subjunctive and wenn adds the sigh
A question, because the inverted order would have to be answered by the listener
options.misconception: believes a clause that opens with wenn must be a yes-or-no question

options.text: A command, because the second subjunctive may stand in for the imperative in a strong wish
options.misconception: believes the second subjunctive can replace the imperative of a command

options.text: A concession, because the wenn-clause states a fact the speaker then takes back
options.misconception: believes a conditional clause is denying the truth of its own content

questions.explanation: Wenn ich nur mehr Zeit hätte is a wish, and two signals make it one: the particle nur in the middle of the clause and the second subjunctive of the verb. The particle is what turns the condition into a lament, since Wenn ich mehr Zeit habe stays a plain statement about the future while Wenn ich nur mehr Zeit hätte says that the speaker treats the time as unavailable and does not expect that to change. German does not use this clause as a command, so a learner who expects an imperative meaning has imported the pattern of a wish in another language. The sentence is also elliptical in the sense that it leaves out any main clause at all, and that is normal here, since a wish is allowed to stand on its own.
questions.hint: Ask what the particle nur adds to an otherwise ordinary condition.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Konjunktiv II in a wish
questions.learningObjective: read a wish and then recast it as a real plan
questions.stem: Stage one: take 'Wenn ich nur einen eigenen Garten hätte!' and say what the form hätte marks and what the particle nur contributes. Stage two: rewrite the wish as a plan the speaker has actually made, keeping tense and mood honest.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: hätte is the second subjunctive of haben and marks a condition the speaker treats as counterfactual, while nur signals that the speaker is not working towards the condition but lamenting it. Stage two: the honest rewrite states a real intention in the ordinary present, so 'Ich lege im Frühjahr ein Beet an' is expected, as is 'Wenn ich im Frühjahr Zeit habe, lege ich ein Beet an', which uses the present for a real condition.

questions.explanation: The two stages are worth pairing because the rewrite is where the mood usually survives by accident. Hätte is the second subjunctive of haben, and in a wish it presents the condition as one the speaker does not expect to be met, while the particle nur adds the sigh that separates this from a plain condition. Turning the wish into a plan means giving up the counterfactual altogether, because a real intention is stated in the present, as in 'Ich lege im Frühjahr ein Beet an', or with a real condition, as in 'Wenn ich im Frühjahr Zeit habe, lege ich ein Beet an'. Keeping the second subjunctive in the rewrite would still describe a situation the speaker has not got, and a learner who reached for the simple past instead would be claiming that a garden existed once and no longer does.
questions.hint: Ask whether the speaker is lamenting the condition or planning to meet it.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The würde form and its limits
questions.learningObjective: say what the würde form stands in for and what it cannot reach
questions.stem: Stage one: take 'Ich würde gern mit dem früheren Zug fahren.' and say what the würde form is standing in for. Stage two: rewrite the wish with the bare second-subjunctive form, and say which kind of past the würde construction cannot express.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: würde is standing in for the second subjunctive of fahren, which would be führe, and the writer prefers the würde form. Stage two: 'Ich führe gern mit dem früheren Zug' is the expected recasting, while a würde sentence cannot reach a past, as in 'Ich würde gern mit dem früheren Zug gefahren sein', which leaves the second part of the past outside the mood.

questions.explanation: The würde form is a substitute rather than a mood of its own: it stands in for a second subjunctive built on the stem, so würde fahren is read as führe fahren. That is why it is convenient in speech and why it fails in two places. A learner cannot use it for a past, since a sentence like 'Ich würde gern mit dem früheren Zug gefahren sein' puts the second part of the perfect outside the mood, and a speaker who means that an earlier evening would have turned out otherwise needs the bare form on an auxiliary instead. And a learner gains nothing from it with the very common verbs that have no vowel change, since those already carry a full second-subjunctive form of their own.
questions.hint: Ask which stem the würde form is covering up, and then ask how far that stem reaches.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Konjunktiv I without a distinct form
questions.learningObjective: explain when a report may lose its mood and what is reached for instead
questions.stem: A learner asks why a textbook writes 'Der Trainer sagt, das Spiel sei hart.' but also 'Der Trainer sagt, das Spiel ist hart.' Explain when the first subjunctive may be left out in a report, and what a writer reaches for when the mood would otherwise be invisible.

answer.exemplar: A report keeps the first subjunctive whenever the verb has a shape of its own, so sein gives sei against the present ist and the reader can see that the claim belongs to the trainer. For a verb such as kommen or sagen the first subjunctive is spelled exactly like the present and the writing carries no signal, so the reporting frame alone has to do the work, and in speech intonation takes over. The fallback is then the second subjunctive, in the bare form or in the würde construction, as in 'Der Trainer sagt, das Spiel wäre hart' or 'Der Trainer sagt, das Spiel würde hart sein'.

questions.explanation: The two shapes in the question differ because of what the verb is doing. Sein has a first subjunctive of its own, sei, so the first version marks the claim as the trainer's, while the second version quietly adopts it, which in a report is a change of responsibility. A verb like kommen or sagen has no separate shape, so its first subjunctive is spelled exactly as the present and the reader has nothing to see; in writing the reporting frame is then the only signal, and in speech intonation carries what the letters cannot. The remedy a course reaches for is the second subjunctive, either the bare form with the umlaut or the würde form, since both are visible on the page, and a learner who uses only the bare form will sound bookish in conversation while one who uses only würde writes a mood the older register avoids.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two versions still lets a reader tell who is claiming what.

questions.topic: A coordinated clause
questions.learningObjective: join two main clauses and keep the word order of each half
questions.stem: A writer has 'Ich rufe dich an.' and 'Du schickst mir die Datei.' and wants one sentence. Which join is correct?

options.text: Ich rufe dich an und du schickst mir die Datei, because each half keeps its own second-position verb
Ich rufe dich an, du schickst mir die Datei, because a comma on its own joins two main clauses
options.misconception: believes a comma on its own is enough to join two main clauses in German

options.text: Ich und du schickst mir die Datei, because one subject can serve two conjugated verbs
options.misconception: believes a single subject can serve two conjugated verbs in one clause

options.text: Ich rufe dich, und an du schickst mir die Datei, because und may stand inside a verb group
options.misconception: believes the conjunction und may be placed inside the verb group of a clause

questions.explanation: Two main clauses joined with und remain two clauses, and each one keeps the word order it had on its own, so the finite verb of the second half takes the second position inside that half and starts with a lower-case du. What und may not do is separate the parts of a verb group, which is why a construction that puts it between anrufen and its prefix can never be right, however natural the break sounds when read aloud. A comma is not enough to join two main clauses in German as it is in English, because a comma in a main clause marks a pause rather than a structural break, and a reader will stop at it expecting a second main clause that never comes. Three clauses are joined in the same way, with und repeated before each of them.
questions.hint: Ask whether each half can still stand on its own as a sentence.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A coordinated clause
questions.learningObjective: screen sentences for the coordination a speaker would accept
questions.stem: A writing drill lists five sentences and reports that three of them are ones a German speaker would accept unchanged. Which three are those?

options.text: Ich komme später und bringe Brot mit
Er ist müde, weil er früh aufstand
Ich komme später, ich bringe Brot mit
options.misconception: joins two main clauses with a comma alone, which German does not allow

options.text: Weil er früh aufstand, ist müde er
options.misconception: puts the subject after the verb inside a subordinate clause it cannot follow

options.text: Weil er früh aufstand, ist er müde

questions.explanation: Three of the five are sentences a speaker would accept. The first joins two main clauses with und and leaves each half with its own second-position verb, the second is a weil-clause with the conjugated verb at its end, and the third puts that same clause in front of the main clause, which the end position for verbs makes possible. The two rejected sentences each break a different rule. The comma alone cannot join two main clauses, and a reader who stops at it is waiting for a main clause that never arrives. And a subordinate clause that has already given its first position to the conjunction has no place left for anything after the verb, so a subject behind the conjugated verb cannot be right.
questions.hint: Ask which line is a subordinate clause, and where its verb may stand.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A relative clause that refers to a possessor
questions.learningObjective: use a genitive relative pronoun to point at an owner rather than an object
questions.stem: A sentence reads 'Das ist die Kollegin, deren Sohn gerade die Zeitung liest.' Why can the clause not open with der?

options.text: The pronoun has to be genitive, because the clause comments on what the colleague owns and not on her
The pronoun has to be plural, because the clause mentions two people and they have to agree
options.misconception: believes a relative pronoun must be plural whenever two people are mentioned

options.text: The pronoun has to be nominative, because every German relative clause opens in that case
options.misconception: believes every German relative clause has to open in the nominative case

options.text: The pronoun has to be left out, because German has no way of pointing at an owner in a clause
options.misconception: believes German has no way of pointing at the owner of a noun inside a clause

questions.explanation: When a relative clause comments on what belongs to the noun rather than on the noun itself, the pronoun stands in the genitive, so deren carries the genitive of die and the clause is about the son this colleague has. The four shapes of the genitive relative pronoun are dessen, deren, dessen and deren, and which one is needed is decided by the gender and the number of the owner, exactly as for any other case. Der would point at the colleague instead, and the sentence would then claim that she is the one reading the paper, which is a different claim rather than a clumsy version of the same one. A learner who has learned the accusative forms well will reach for the one that looks familiar.
questions.hint: Ask whether the clause is about the person or about something that person owns.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A purpose clause with um ... zu
questions.learningObjective: build a purpose clause whose subject is the subject of the main clause
questions.stem: A writer wants to say that she is learning German in order to work in Austria. Which sentence is correct?

options.text: Ich lerne Deutsch, um in Österreich zu arbeiten, because the two clauses share one subject
Ich lerne Deutsch, um ich in Österreich arbeiten, because a purpose clause keeps its own subject
options.misconception: believes a purpose clause with um ... zu may contain a subject of its own

options.text: Ich lerne Deutsch, damit ich in Österreich arbeiten kann, because a purpose clause needs a second subject
options.misconception: believes a purpose clause whose subject matches the main subject has to use damit

options.text: Ich lerne Deutsch, zu um in Österreich zu arbeiten, because the two forms of a purpose clause combine
options.misconception: believes the um form and the damit form may be used together inside one clause

questions.explanation: The form um ... zu is a purpose clause whose subject is the same as the subject of the main clause, which is why zu has to be followed by a verb with no subject of its own, and why a speaker who needs a different subject uses damit instead. The two forms are therefore chosen by whether the subjects match and not by taste, and nothing is gained by mixing them in one clause. A second restriction is that um ... zu may not stand in the first position, so the sentence has to be rearranged, as in Um in Österreich zu arbeiten, lerne ich Deutsch, which is possible but marked. The same restriction is why a purpose clause cannot simply be added to a modal sentence.
questions.hint: Ask whether the person who works in Austria is the person who is learning German.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A purpose clause with damit
questions.learningObjective: choose damit where the subject of the purpose differs from the main subject
questions.stem: A writer wants to say that she is learning German so that her brother can get work in Austria. Which sentence is correct?

options.text: Ich lerne Deutsch, damit mein Bruder in Österreich arbeiten kann, because the two clauses have different subjects
Ich lerne Deutsch, um mein Bruder in Österreich arbeiten kann, because a purpose clause needs its own subject
options.misconception: believes the um form covers a purpose clause whose subject differs from the main subject

options.text: Ich lerne Deutsch, damit mein Bruder in Österreich zu arbeiten kann, because damit also takes zu before the verb
options.misconception: believes the damit form of a purpose clause also requires the particle zu before the verb

options.text: Ich lerne Deutsch, meinem Bruder in Österreich zu arbeiten, because a purpose clause needs no conjunction
options.misconception: believes a purpose clause can be written as a bare infinitive with no conjunction at all

questions.explanation: Damit is the form of a purpose clause for the case where the subject of the purpose is not the subject of the main clause, which is exactly the situation here, since the speaker is the one learning and the brother is the one who would work. The clause therefore needs a subject of its own, and it closes with the conjugated verb in the ordinary subordinate order, so the modal kann is what a reader expects to find at the end. The um ... zu form cannot be used, because its two clauses would have to share a subject that they do not share, and putting zu into the damit clause produces a form German does not use. The test is to ask whether the two clauses are about the same person, and the answer decides between the two forms.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two clauses are about the same person or about two people.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A single word that changes the claim
questions.learningObjective: read what one added word does to the attitude behind a sentence
questions.stem: A review says 'Die neue Software ist komplett.' and a second version says 'Die neue Software ist leider komplett.' What has the added word done?

options.text: It has turned a plain statement of fact into a regret, and the fact itself is unchanged
It has turned a statement of fact into a guess about what the writer supposes to be true
options.misconception: believes a single added word can turn a statement into a reported guess about facts

options.text: It has turned a statement of fact into an order, and the reader is now being told to act
options.misconception: believes a single added word can turn a plain statement into an order to the reader

options.text: It has turned a statement of fact into a question, and the writer is asking the reader to confirm it
options.misconception: believes a single added word can turn a plain statement into a question to the reader

questions.explanation: Adding leider to a statement of fact adds no information, because the fact itself has not changed, and what it changes is the attitude the writer takes towards it: the sentence now says that the writer wishes the opposite were the case. A reader who is collecting content will miss the whole thing, and that is why a reading test can turn on one short word. The same weight sits on a particle that contradicts a clause, as in Das ist ja nicht mein Fach, where ja asks the reader to accept something the writer knows to be untrue, and on position, as in Der Bericht ist nicht fertig against a phrase that puts nicht at the end, which no speaker would say and which exists only to show that the first position is not free. The habit worth building is to read for the claim before collecting details.
questions.hint: Ask whether the added word carries a fact or an attitude towards the fact.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A single word that changes the claim
questions.learningObjective: compare two versions of a report and name the change in the claim itself
questions.stem: Two lines of a report are set side by side: 'Die Bahn hat den Ausbau der Strecke vorgezogen.' and 'Die Bahn hat den Ausbau der Strecke nicht vorgezogen.' What has changed between them?

options.text: Only the claim itself, because the second line denies the single action the first line reported
Only the tone, because the second line reports the same action in a more cautious way
options.misconception: believes adding a negation can soften a report without changing what it claims

options.text: Only the time of the action, because the second line moves the work to a later date
options.misconception: believes a negated verb phrase pushes the time of the action to a later date

options.text: Only the agent of the action, because the second line names a different body as responsible
options.misconception: believes a negated verb phrase hands the action to a different responsible body

questions.explanation: One inserted word can reverse a claim entirely, and Nicht is the most economical example there is, since the first line says the work has been brought forward while the second says it has not. Nothing about the time, the place or the agent has changed: the same body, the same project and the same verb stand in both lines, and the difference is a flat contradiction. A reader who is collecting dates will take the second line for a variant of the first, and the same trap is set by a modal, as in a line with könnte, which introduces a possibility rather than a fact. The habit worth building is to read a sentence for its claim before collecting any of its details.
questions.hint: Ask which single word a reader could delete to make one line say the opposite.
